METHODS: We evaluated the effects of BBM on MDA-MB-231, MDA-MB-468, MCF-7, and 4T1 breast cancer cells and normal mammary epithelial cells using assays of cell viability, migration, invasion, autophagy-related responses, lysosome-associated changes, immunofluorescence, transmission electron microscopy, and Western blotting. Exploratory network analysis was used to prioritize candidate BBM-associated pathways, and molecular docking was used to predict interactions between BBM and selected pathway proteins. Antitumor activity was further assessed in an MCF-7 xenograft model. RESULTS: BBM inhibited the proliferation, migration, and invasion of breast cancer cells while showing relatively low cytotoxicity toward normal mammary epithelial cells. BBM treatment was associated with increased levels of p-ULK1, ATG5, ATG7, and Beclin1, increased LC3 puncta, and accumulation of double-membraned autophagosomes. BBM was also associated with TFEB nuclear translocation, increased LAMP2 expression, and enhanced LysoTracker staining. Network analysis prioritized the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, and molecular docking predicted potential interactions between BBM and PI3K, Akt1, and mTOR. Western blot analysis showed reduced phosphorylation of these proteins in cultured breast cancer cells. In the MCF-7 xenograft model, BBM inhibited tumor growth and was associated with changes in autophagy-related markers. DISCUSSION: These findings support the involvement of autophagy-related responses, lysosome-associated changes, and PI3K/Akt1/mTOR pathway modulation in the anti-breast-cancer effects of BBM, while further studies are needed to establish direct target engagement and causal relationships.

articles.title: PCSK9 inhibitor use and risk of dementia and neurodegenerative diseases in adults aged 50 Years and older: a global electronic health record study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors achieve profound lipid lowering, yet their long-term neurocognitive effects remain uncertain. Evidence from randomized trials is limited by short follow-up and lack of dedicated neurodegenerative endpoints. METHODS: We performed a retrospective target trial emulation using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network. Adults aged ≥50 years with hyperlipidemia initiating PCSK9 inhibitors or comparator lipid-lowering therapies between 2015 and 2024 were included. Active-comparator cohorts were constructed against statins, ezetimibe, and fenofibrate or cholestyramine with mutual exclusion of prior exposure. Propensity score matching at a 1:1 ratio balanced demographics, body mass index, socioeconomic indicators, healthcare utilization, and cardiometabolic comorbidities. Outcomes included incident all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease, and other neurodegenerative disorders. Sensitivity analyses incorporated lag periods, varying follow-up durations, alternative matching strategies, and intention-to-treat analyses. Cross-dataset validation was additionally conducted using the US Collaborative Network to assess reproducibility under independent data settings. Hazard ratio along with 95% confidence interval were evaluated in each analysis. RESULTS: Among 31,604 matched PCSK9 inhibitor-statin pairs, PCSK9 inhibitor use was associated with lower risks of all-cause dementia (HR 0.454; 95% CI 0.394-0.522), Alzheimer's disease (HR 0.553; 95% CI 0.433-0.705), vascular dementia (HR 0.536; 95% CI 0.402-0.714), Parkinson's disease (HR 0.686; 95% CI 0.544-0.865), and other neurodegenerative disorders (HR 0.730; 95% CI 0.645-0.825). Results were consistent across comparator therapies, cross-dataset validation and sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSION: PCSK9 inhibitor use was associated with lower observed risks of neurodegenerative outcomes across multiple analyses and datasets. These findings support a potential association but do not establish causality and require confirmation in prospective trials.

articles.title: Early postmarketing reporting patterns of resmetirom in FAERS: disproportionality analyses with indication-restricted and active comparators.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Resmetirom is the first approved liver-directed thyroid hormone receptor-beta agonist for noncirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with fibrosis. Early liver-event reporting may be distorted by indication leakage (the treated disease or its manifestations recorded as adverse events), disease progression, and surveillance bias. METHODS: We analyzed FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) data from 2024Q1 through 2026Q1. Deduplicated primary- or secondary-suspect reports were assessed at preferred-term, system-organ-class, and nine predefined clinical-cluster levels using frequentist and Bayesian disproportionality metrics. References included all FAERS, US MASH-indication reports, and an exploratory 144-report active comparator. Sensitivity analyses examined cirrhosis indications, serious outcomes, onset-data selection, and co-medications. RESULTS: Among 3,155,054 deduplicated cases, 1,429 resmetirom reports were analyzed. Versus all non-resmetirom reports, RORs (95% CIs) were 12.13 (10.61-13.88) for hepatocellular injury and 11.46 (9.24-14.21) for cholestasis/biliary events. Gastrointestinal, thyroid/metabolic, and rash/hypersensitivity reporting was also enriched. Hepatic estimates remained elevated after excluding 35 cirrhosis-indication reports and in restricted comparisons, although sparse cells produced wide confidence intervals. The active comparator comprised 142 GLP-1/GIP and two pioglitazone reports. Against this reference, RORs were 1.36 (0.93-1.99) for gastrointestinal intolerance, 0.93 (0.59-1.47) for nausea, 1.42 (0.18-11.18) for cholelithiasis, and 1.95 (1.12-3.41) for diarrhoea. The first three attenuated, whereas diarrhoea remained elevated. Only 206 reports (14.4%) had valid exact onset dates, with systematic differences from reports lacking dates. Sex was missing in 94.6%. Gemfibrozil and clopidogrel were co-reported in three and 25 cases, respectively. CONCLUSION: Early FAERS reporting patterns recapitulated recognized gastrointestinal, hepatic, biliary, cutaneous, and thyroid/metabolic domains. Comparator-dependent attenuation suggests that crude all-FAERS estimates partly reflect treatment-context reporting. However, the small GLP-1/GIP-dominant comparator, missing data, target-organ confounding, and spontaneous-report limitations preclude incidence, comparative-risk, or causal inference. These hypothesis-generating patterns support clinical monitoring and denominator-based confirmation.

articles.title: Protective effect of melatonin on intestinal mucosal injury in intermittent hypoxic rats.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effects of melatonin (MT) on intestinal mucosal injury associated with intermittent hypoxic (HI) in rats. METHODS: Thirty-six male Wistar rats were randomly divided into control (Ctrl), HI, MT groups (n = 12 per group). Each group was further divided into 2- and 4-week subgroups (n = 6 per group per time point), with different animals used at the two terminal sampling time points. Rats in the Ctrl group were exposed to compressed air, whereas rats in the HI and MT groups underwent intermittent hypoxia for 7 h daily. MT (20 mg/kg) was administered intraperitoneally before each daily exposure, while rats in the Ctrl and HI groups received an equivalent volume of vehicle. At the designated 2- or 4-week endpoint, the sampling procedure was initiated immediately after completion of the final daily exposure. Small intestinal tissue and central venous blood were collected. Intestinal histopathological changes were assessed by hematoxylin and eosin staining and Chiu scoring, and villus area, height, thickness, and crypt depth were measured. Serum ROS, MDA, SOD, and DAO levels were determined. RESULT: Intermittent hypoxia was associated with intestinal histopathological injury and significant reductions in villus area, villus height, villus thickness, and crypt depth at both 2 and 4 weeks. At 2 weeks, no significant differences in villus morphometric parameters were observed between the MT and HI groups, at 4 weeks, villus area and height were significantly greater in the MT group than in the HI group. At 2 weeks, SOD activity was significantly higher in the MT group than in the HI group, whereas ROS, MDA, and DAO levels did not differ significantly between these groups. At 4 weeks, the MT group showed significantly lower ROS, MDA, and DAO levels and significantly higher SOD activity than the HI group. Histological findings also indicated less severe intestinal mucosal injury in MT-treated rats. CONCLUSION: Intermittent hypoxia was associated with intestinal mucosal injury and changes in oxidative stress-related biochemical indicators in rats. Melatonin treatment was associated with attenuation of histopathological injury and a more favorable biochemical profile, with these differences being more evident at 4 weeks.

articles.title: Modulatory effect of Canavalia gladiata lectin on quinolone activity against multidrug-resistant and efflux pump-positive Staphylococcus aureus.
articles.abstract: Clinically relevant bacteria have increasingly developed resistance to antimicrobial agents, reducing the effectiveness of conventional antibiotic therapies. In this context, antibiotic adjuvants capable of restoring or enhancing the activity of existing drugs represent a potential strategy against multidrug-resistant bacteria. This study evaluated the potential of a lectin isolated from Canavalia gladiata seeds (CGL) as an antibiotic-modulating agent against multidrug-resistant and efflux pump-positive bacterial strains. CGL was purified by affinity chromatography on Sephadex G-50, and its direct antibacterial activity was evaluated by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Its modulatory effects were subsequently assessed in combination with conventional antibiotics and in assays involving strains carrying the NorA and MepA efflux pumps. CGL showed weak intrinsic antibacterial activity against all tested strains, with MIC values ≥1,024 μg/mL. However, when used at a sub-inhibitory concentration, CGL moderately enhanced the activity of norfloxacin against Staphylococcus aureus 10, reducing the MIC from 256 to 170.6 μg/mL, and ciprofloxacin against S. aureus K2068, reducing the MIC from 32 to 13.3 μg/mL. These effects did not restore bacterial susceptibility to clinically established therapeutic breakpoints. In contrast, no significant enhancement was observed for the other antibiotic combinations, and some associations resulted in increased MIC values. Therefore, CGL does not appear to act as a direct antibacterial agent under the conditions evaluated, but may have potential as an antibiotic adjuvant, particularly in combination with quinolones against selected S. aureus strains. Further mechanistic, toxicity, and in vivo studies are required to determine its applicability as an antibiotic-modulating agent.

articles.title: Tofacitinib laden MCM-48 mesoporous silica nanogel for topical psoriasis: ex vivo and in vivo therapeutic validation.
articles.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory skin disorder wherein conventional therapies are frequently constrained by poor percutaneous absorption, high recurrence rates, and systemic or steroid-induced adverse effects. This study developed Tofacitinib-loaded MCM-48 mesoporous silica nanoparticles (TFC-MCM-48) incorporated into a Carbopol hydrogel as a topical nanocarrier system for controlled TFC delivery. Blank MCM-48 MSNs were optimized using a Box-Behnken design, followed by TFC loading through modified solvent evaporation and hydrogel formulation. A validated RP-HPLC method was used for TFC quantification. The optimized blank MCM-48 exhibited particle size of 251.8 ± 12.3 nm (PDI 0.172 ± 0.02), shifting to 311.6 ± 17.2 nm (PDI 0.326 ± 0.03) upon drug loading. Nitrogen adsorption porosimetry and low-angle XRD supported TFC incorporation with retention of the ordered mesoporous architecture and reduced drug crystallinity. The formulated TFC-MCM-48 gel was homogeneous, with a viscosity of 27,800 ± 225 cP and spreadability of 16.91 ± 0.24 g·cm/s, providing sustained in vitro release of ∼54% and greater ex vivo permeation across excised skin of ∼50% over 12 h, which maintained the physicochemical and release performance across three months of storage. In a cyclophosphamide-imiquimod-induced psoriasiform BALB/c mouse model, TFC-MCM-48 gel significantly outperformed pure drug gel, achieving a ∼92% reduction in PASI score than disease control, reducing epidermal thickness and Baker's histopathological score. This recovery was accompanied by marked attenuation of serum C-reactive protein, splenomegaly, and liver weight indices, with improved skin and spleen histology. These findings highlight TFC-MCM-48 hydrogel as a promising topical nanoplatform for Psoriasis management.

articles.title: Prim-O-glucosylcimifugin alleviates silica-induced pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway.
articles.abstract: Silicosis is an irreversible occupational interstitial lung disease characterized primarily by inflammation and diffuse pulmonary fibrosis, for which effective drug treatments are currently lacking. Prim-O-glucosylcimifugin (POG) exhibits anti-inflammatory effects, but its effectiveness in treating silicosis is not yet determined. This study combines network pharmacology with experimental validation to investigate the protective effects of POG against early- and late-stage silica-induced lung inflammation and fibrosis, as well as the underlying mechanisms. Specifically, results from a network pharmacology analysis revealed that 58 overlapping targets were identified between POG and silicosis; among these, the PI3K/ AKT signaling pathway plays a key role in mediating the therapeutic effect of POG against silicosis. Furthermore, in vivo studies demonstrated that POG significantly mitigated silica-induced lung injury and respiratory dysfunction, inhibited pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6), and decreased both pulmonary hydroxyproline levels and fibrosis-related protein expression (collagen I and fibronectin). Significantly, these strong protective effects were dose-dependent, irrespective of whether POG was given early (day 2) or late (day 14) after modeling. Cellular experiments confirmed that POG downregulated inflammatory and fibrotic markers in fibroblasts. Mechanistically, POG effectively inhibited the activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway; crucially, the co-administration of the PI3K agonist 740Y-P completely offset its protective anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects. Ultimately, the results of this study indicate that POG effectively alleviates silica-induced pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. These findings provide compelling preclinical evidence and a pharmacological basis for the potential application of POG in the treatment of silicosis.

articles.title: In vitro cell model to assess human erythro-megakaryocytic lineage- and stage-specific toxicity of new antitumoral metallic complexes.
articles.abstract: Early preclinical assessment of hematotoxicity is essential to minimize extensive ex vivo and in vivo experimentation during antitumoral drug development. The erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages are particularly sensitive to chemotherapeutic agents, and reductions in red blood cells or platelets often require treatment interruption or dose adjustment. Therefore, reliable in vitro models capable of detecting lineage-specific toxicity across different stages of maturation can be highly valuable. We developed a in vitro model based on the human cell lines K562 and HEL, which phenotypically resemble bipotential erythro-megakaryocytic progenitors and can be induced to undergo erythroid or megakaryocytic differentiation using defined agents. Cells were characterized in progenitor and differentiated states by viability assays, flow cytometric analysis of DNA content, immunophenotyping, and morphological assessment. Prototype metal-based compounds developed by our group (iodido‑platinum, phosphine‑platinum, and thiosemicarbazone‑copper complexes) were tested at different stages of differentiation. The model discriminated between erythroid and megakaryocytic toxicity among different compounds, lineages, and maturation stages. Differential sensitivity was observed depending on both the drug tested and the differentiation stage. Toxicity could be assessed in single cultures or co-culture conditions. This simple and cost-effective in vitro cell platform enables rapid and reliable detection of erythro-megakaryocytic toxicity in novel antitumoral agents and may help optimize preclinical drug evaluation strategies.

articles.title: Study on the toxic effects of benzopyrene exposure on umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells and the mitigating effects of folic acid.
articles.abstract: Benzo[a]pyrene (BaP) is a potent mutagen and human carcinogen. BaP has been shown to cause a variety of cytotoxicities. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (HUC-MSCs) play important roles in tissue regeneration and the treatment of various diseases because of their pluripotent differentiation and self-renewal abilities, immunomodulatory effects, and long-term proliferation in vitro. However, to date, no specific studies have investigated the toxic effects of BaP on HUC-MSCs. Folic acid (FA) participates in one‑carbon metabolism in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, mediating the transfer of one‑carbon units and playing a crucial role in nucleotide synthesis, methylation, and amino acid balance. Folic acid has been demonstrated to inhibit the toxicity of BaP both in vivo and in vitro. Therefore, we selected human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (HUC-MSCs) as our research model to investigate the effects of benzo[a]pyrene exposure on cultured human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells and the reparative effects of folic acid against benzo[a]pyrene exposure. We aimed to evaluate these effects through CCK-8 assays, comet assays, γH2AX immunofluorescence staining, reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection, FITC-luciferase coupled Annexin-V double staining, alizarin red staining, oil red O staining, and RT-qPCR to evaluate BaP's toxic effects on cell viability, DNA damage, oxidative stress, apoptosis, osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation, as well as folic acid's reparative effects against these toxicities. Results demonstrated that BaP exposure significantly reduced HUC-MSC survival rates, exacerbated DNA damage and oxidative stress levels, induced apoptosis, caused abnormalities in osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation, and disrupted the normal differentiation process of HUC-MSCs. Conversely, FA mitigated BaP-induced DNA damage and oxidative stress in HUC-MSCs, enhanced the expression of antioxidant-related genes, suppressed apoptosis, and alleviated the abnormal osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation, but failed to reverse the BaP-induced upregulation of apoptosis-related genes. In a word, our findings provide crucial experimental evidence for exploring the mechanism of benzo[a]pyrene's toxicity on human umbilical cord blood mesenchymal stem cells, thereby offering a basis for developing BaP prevention strategies.

articles.title: Vericiguat attenuates cardiac inflammation and oxidative stress in an obese postmenopausal rat model with concurrent modulation of PKG-I, TGF-β1, and NF-κB.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Inflammation and oxidative stress are implicated in cardiometabolic changes associated with menopause and obesity. This study investigated the effects of Vericiguat (VER) alone and in combination with estradiol (E2) on oxidative, inflammatory, atherogenic and fibrosis-related markers in cardiac tissue in an ovariectomized rat model of diet-induced obesity. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Female Wistar rats were divided into sham and ovariectomized (OVX) groups and fed a standard diet (SD) or high-fat diet (HFD) for 4 months, followed by 4 weeks of treatment with E2, two doses of VER, or their combination. Body weight, malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), plasma atherogenic index (AIP), cardiac risk indices I and II (CRI-I and CRI-II), cardiac hydroxyproline, and expression of cardiac PKG-I, NF-κB, and TGF-β1 proteins were assessed. RESULTS: OVX and HFD were associated with increased body weight, AIP, CRI-I, CRI-II, MDA, cardiac NF-κB and TGF-β1 expression, and hydroxyproline content, along with decreased TAC, TAC/MDA ratio, and PKG-I expression. E2 and VER treatments improved these alterations, as evidenced by reductions in AIP, CRI-I, CRI-II, MDA, NF-κB, TGF-β1, and hydroxyproline, as well as increases in TAC, TAC/MDA ratio, and PKG-I expression. Combined treatment with E2 and VER, compared to treatment with E2 alone, significantly improved all these parameters, with the exception of CRI-I and CRI-II. There were significant interactions between E2 and VER treatments were observed for TAC/MDA, hydroxyproline content, and TGF-β1 expression. CONCLUSION: VER and E2 ameliorated several oxidative, inflammatory, atherogenic, and fibrosis-related changes in this model.

articles.title: Targeting Seizures and Neurobehavioral Alterations: Efficacy of Brivaracetam-Sertraline Combination in PTZ-Induced Kindling Model.
articles.abstract: Epilepsy is a neurological disorder associated with various psychiatric comorbidities, among which anxiety and depressive disorders are most prevalent. These psychiatric comorbidities remain frequently untreated due to concerns about exacerbation of seizures and limited awareness about antidepressant selection. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of brivaracetam (BRV) and sertraline (SRT) administered alone and in combination on the progression of seizures and associated behavioral changes. Male BALB/c mice were subjected to the pentylenetetrazol (PTZ)-induced kindling process followed by behavioral tests to examine the impact of test treatments on kindling-associated anxiety, cognitive deficit, and depressive disorders. Subsequently, the brains were dissected, and oxidative stress was estimated in brain homogenates; histopathological studies were also carried out to monitor changes in the hippocampal regions. The combination of BRV and SRT attenuated seizure development and progression and markedly protected the mice from cognitive impairment, as their discrimination indices were increased in novel object recognition test together with longer step-through latencies in the passive avoidance test. Anxiety and depression-like behavior were notably ameliorated in mice treated with BRV+SRT combination, along with reduction in oxidative stress and histopathological alterations in the hippocampi. The combination of BRV and SRT exerted enhanced therapeutic benefits in reducing seizures and improving behavioral changes as compared to BRV or SRT administered alone. Our findings suggest that combining sertraline with antiseizure medications may provide a promising strategy to manage seizures and psychiatric disorders in epileptic patients, warranting more preclinical and clinical investigations to enhance patients' quality of life with comorbid psychiatric disorders.

articles.title: Multi-omics and pharmacological analyses identify DDX60 as a candidate EGCG-engaged target in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is highly aggressive with limited available biomarkers, and discovering causative, functionally significant, and pharmacologically tractable targets is fundamental for new intervention strategies. By integrating Mendelian randomization, multi-cohort transcriptomic validation, single-cell analysis, and experimental pharmacology, DDX60 was identified as a key candidate gene associated with ESCC. The two-sample MR integrating eQTLGen, IEU OpenGWAS, and FinnGen datasets identified DDX60 as a key gene associated with esophageal cancer. Multi-omics utilizing TCGA, GTEx, cfDNA 5hmC profiling, and paired clinical ESCC specimens validated DDX60 expression in ESCC. Single-cell RNA-seq showed DDX60 enrichment in tumor-derived malignant epithelial cells versus matched normal epithelium. Epithelial cells expressing high DDX60 displayed enhanced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and interferon-response signatures, accompanied by a slightly elevated PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway score and progression along the malignant epithelial trajectory. Functionally, silencing DDX60 in ESCC cells increased apoptosis, decreased the phosphorylation of PI3K, AKT, and mTOR, and inhibited migration and invasion. These results demonstrated the role of DDX60 in ESCC progression. To explore potential pharmacological modulation of DDX60, PheWAS- and DSigDB-guided compound screening, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulation were performed, identifying epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG) as a candidate DDX60-associated compound. EGCG reduced ESCC cell viability, decreased the levels of DDX60 protein, and enhanced the thermal stability of endogenous DDX60 in cell-based CETSA assays. Analysis using DDX60-knockdown cells further suggested that DDX60 status may influence cellular responsiveness to EGCG. Conclusively, DDX60 demonstrated considerable potential as an exploitable target in ESCC, amenable to modulation by EGCG through the disruption of DDX60-associated oncogenic mechanisms.

articles.title: Sanmiao San Attenuates D-galactose-induced Chondrocyte Senescence by Regulating the FoxM1-p21 Signaling Pathway.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Sanmiao San (SMS), a traditional Chinese medicine formula, is commonly used to treat Bi syndrome and has been widely applied in the clinical management of knee osteoarthritis (KOA) in China. However, its protective effects against cartilage degeneration and chondrocyte senescence, as well as the underlying molecular mechanisms, remain to be fully elucidated. AIM OF THE STUDY: To investigate the inhibitory effects of SMS on D-galactose (D-gal)-induced chondrocyte senescence and to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms and primary active components of SMS. MATERIALS AND METHODS: D-gal-induced senescence models were established in a human chondrocyte cell line and rat primary chondrocytes. Cellular senescence was assessed by senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) staining. Colony formation assays were performed to evaluate the clonogenic capacity of chondrocytes. Proteoglycan secretion was evaluated by toluidine blue staining. γ-H2A.X expression was assessed by immunofluorescence. Cell cycle arrest was analyzed by flow cytometry. Transcriptomic analysis was performed to identify differentially expressed genes. These genes were annotated using the CellAge database to screen for senescence-related genes and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) factors. Key SASP factors were further validated by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were measured by fluorescence assay. The expression of Forkhead box M1 (FoxM1) and p21 was analyzed by quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), Western blotting and immunofluorescence. The prototype constituents and metabolites of SMS in rat serum were identified by ultra-performance liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS). RESULTS: SMS-containing serum (SMS-CS) attenuated D-gal-induced chondrocyte senescence by reducing the proportion of SA-β-gal-positive cells, downregulating p21 and γ-H2A.X expression, alleviating cell cycle arrest and promoting colony formation. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that SMS-CS upregulated most genes annotated as downregulated during senescence and downregulated a subset of those annotated as upregulated during senescence in the CellAge database. SMS-CS also modulated most SASP factors, particularly interleukin-6 (IL-6) and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), as further confirmed by ELISA. KEGG and GO enrichment analysis of specific drug targets revealed significant enrichment in cell cycle, mitotic processes and cellular senescence, while comprehensive bioinformatics analysis predicted FoxM1 as a core target. FoxM1 inhibitor intervention showed that SMS-CS significantly counteracted the FoxM1 downregulation-induced increases in SA-β-gal-positive cell percentage, p21 mRNA levels, γ-H2A.X expression, ROS levels and SASP secretion, as well as the FoxM1 downregulation-induced decrease in proteoglycan secretion, thereby attenuating chondrocyte senescence progression. UPLC-MS analysis identified the following major prototype components and metabolites of SMS in rat serum: Ferulic acid, Esculetin, Atractyloside A, Inokosterone, 20,26-Dihydroxyecdysone, trans-Ferulic acid + hydroxy, Obacunone + hydroxy, and Atractylenolide III + hydroxy. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that the FoxM1-p21 axis may be involved in the anti-senescence effects of SMS-CS in chondrocytes and could represent a potential therapeutic target for KOA.

articles.title: Dimeric procyanidins attenuate matrix metalloproteinase-2 activity and suppress colorectal cancer cell invasion.
articles.abstract: Matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) is a key extracellular protease involved in extracellular matrix degradation and colorectal cancer (CRC) cell invasion. Although dimeric procyanidins (PCA) epicatechin gallate (ECG) dimer and epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) dimer, have been reported to attenuate CRC cell invasion, their capacity to directly modulate MMP-2 activity remains unclear. This work investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying the modulation of MMP-2 activity by ECG and EGCG dimers. Gelatin zymography revealed concentration-dependent reductions in recombinant MMP-2 gelatinolytic activity, with apparent IC50 values of 0.09 and 0.39 μM for ECG and EGCG dimers, respectively. Fluorescence quenching and isothermal titration calorimetry further demonstrated direct interactions between both dimers and MMP-2. Molecular modeling predicted that both dimers could bind near the catalytic region of MMP-2. In CRC cell models, ECG and EGCG dimers significantly decreased MMP-2 mRNA and protein levels while increasing tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-2 (TIMP-2) levels. These effects were accompanied by reduced gelatinase activity and suppression of CRC cell invasion. Collectively, these findings suggest that dimeric PCAs modulate MMP-2-associated gelatinolytic activity and regulate the MMP-2/TIMP-2 axis, providing mechanistic insights for their anti-invasive activity and supporting their potential as modulators of MMP-2-associated processes involved in CRC invasion.

articles.title: Irosustat and STX140 improve cognitive function and modulate amyloid, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways in experimental Alzheimer's disease.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is currently the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder affecting the geriatric population. The pathology of AD has been described as neuronal loss caused by the accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles resulting from tau protein phosphorylation. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of steroid sulfatase inhibition using two drugs, the clinical steroid sulfatase inhibitor Irosustat and the multi-targeting preclinical candidate STX140, in scopolamine-induced AD in male Wistar rats compared to Donepezil as a standard drug. Behavioral tests such as the Open Field Test, Elevated Plus Maze Test, and Morris Water Maze Test were conducted to confirm the disease state and assess any improvement. At the end of the study, the animals were dissected to collect blood and brain samples for morphological, histological, immunohistochemical, biochemical, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting analyses. Treatment with Irosustat or STX140 improved learning, memory, and cognitive function compared with the disease group. The treated groups showed lowered brain tissue Aβ-40 & 42 levels, acetylcholinesterase activity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory markers. Morphological assessments showed that the drugs protected against brain atrophy and neuronal loss. Irosustat and STX140 are therefore promising therapeutic candidates for the management of Alzheimer's Disease.

articles.title: Activation of GLP-1 receptors in the middle part of the paraventricular nucleus of thalamus suppresses alcohol-related responses.
articles.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) remains a major public health challenge, and identifying the brain circuits through which pharmacological interventions act is central to developing more effective treatments. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists suppress alcohol-related behaviors in rodents and reduce alcohol consumption in clinical populations with AUD, yet the neuroanatomical substrates mediating these effects remain only partly mapped. One candidate region implicated in addiction is the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT), particularly its middle part (mid-PVT), which modulates mesolimbic dopamine signaling, has been implicated in addiction-related processes including alcohol use, and expresses GLP-1R. Whether activation of GLP-1R in the mid-PVT influences alcohol-related responses had not been examined, and that was the aim of the present study. Here, we found that local GLP-1R antagonism in the mid-PVT with exendin-3(9-39) (Ex9) attenuated the suppressive effect of systemically administered GLP-1R agonist exendin-4 (Ex4) on alcohol-induced locomotor stimulation, implicating this region in the central actions of GLP-1R agonists. Intra-mid-PVT Ex4 also attenuated alcohol-induced locomotor stimulation and accumbal dopamine release in male mice, without altering the expression of alcohol-induced conditioned place preference. We further showed that Ex4 into the mid-PVT reduced alcohol intake in male and female rats, although a higher dose was required in females. In a separate cohort of alcohol-consuming, treatment-naive rats, Glp1r mRNA in the PVT did not differ between the sexes. Together, these findings indicate that GLP-1R in the mid-PVT contributes to alcohol-related responses, extending the neuroanatomical map of circuits through which GLP-1R agonists may suppress alcohol intake.

articles.title: α7 nicotinic receptors in the ventral tegmental area gate the acute ethanol effects on aversive memory formation.
articles.abstract: Acute ethanol intoxication is classically associated with impairments in memory formation, yet the circuit and receptor mechanisms through which it modulates aversive memory formation remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of a single post-training injection of different binge-like doses of ethanol on memory formation using an inhibitory avoidance task in young adult male rats. An intermediate dose of ethanol (1.5 g/kg) induced the expected memory impairment, whereas a higher dose (2.5 g/kg) produced a long-lasting enhancement of aversive memory formation that persisted for at least 21 days. Both effects depended on α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α7nAChRs) within the ventral tegmental area (VTA). Intra-VTA antagonism of α7nAChRs with methyllycaconitine prevented ethanol-induced memory enhancement, while intra-VTA positive allosteric modulation of α7nAChRs with PNU-120596 prevented the memory impairment produced by the lower dose. In addition, pharmacological activation of prefrontal cortical D1 dopaminergic receptors restored ethanol-induced memory enhancement following intra-VTA α7nAChR antagonism, suggesting that prefrontal cortical D1 receptor signaling is involved in the enhancement pathway. Together, these findings identify VTA α7nAChRs as key regulators of the dose-dependent effects of acute ethanol on aversive memory formation, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how acute alcohol exposure can produce opposing mnemonic outcomes.

articles.title: Cisplatin activates ERK1/2-EGR1-MMP10 axis to promote renal inflammation and injury.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nephrotoxicity caused by cisplatin is a common complication in patients undergoing chemotherapy. This study investigated whether cisplatin induces sustained activation of the extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) and early growth response 1 (EGR1) pathways, thereby modulating the expression of inflammatory mediators and matrix metalloproteinase 10 (MMP10). To address this question, both in vivo and in vitro cisplatin models were employed. METHODS: In the in vivo model, nine-week-old male Balb/c mice received a single intraperitoneal injection of cisplatin (15 mg/kg), diluted in 0.9% saline. They were then compared to control mice that received only 0.9% saline. The mice were euthanized four days later. In vitro experiments were performed using TKPTS cells (a mouse kidney proximal tubular epithelial cell line) treated with cisplatin (25 μM) for 24 h. RESULTS: Cisplatin induced severe proximal tubular injury and inflammation in animals, as well as increased ERK1/2 phosphorylation (pERK1/2) and elevated EGR1 and MMP10 protein immunostaining. Similarly, exposure to cisplatin in vitro induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation and associated upregulation of EGR1 protein and MMP10 transcription. Previously, inhibiting pERK1/2 with the MEK inhibitor PD98059 (2'-amino-3'-methoxyflavone) or knocking down Egr1 in TKPTS cells reduced the expression of inflammatory markers (Il6, Cxcl1 and Cxcl10) and Mmp10. CONCLUSION: Overall, these results suggest that kidney injury in cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity is associated with inflammatory processes and increased MMP10 expression, potentially via the pERK1/2-EGR1-MMP10 signaling pathway.

articles.title: A novel topical formulation with anti-inflammatory potential for localized abrocitinib delivery to atopic dermatitis skin.
articles.abstract: Oral abrocitinib is an effective treatment for atopic dermatitis (AD), but its use may be limited by systemic adverse effects. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a novel liposomes-in-hydrogel system for localized topical delivery of abrocitinib by incorporating abrocitinib-loaded liposomes as drug carriers into a chitosan-based hydrogel (Ab-Lip-Hyd), with the goal of promoting skin retention while limiting transdermal permeation. The formulation was characterized in terms of vesicle size, polydispersity index, zeta potential, entrapment efficiency and storage stability. The developed liposomes exhibited a mean vesicle size of ∼200 nm, a near-neutral surface charge and an entrapment efficiency exceeding 90 %. Incorporation into the hydrogel yielded a physicochemically stable formulation over four weeks of storage. In vitro release studies demonstrated prolonged abrocitinib release from Ab-Lip-Hyd and ex vivo skin permeation studies showed local skin retention with limited transdermal permeation, supporting the intended localized delivery profile. Anti-inflammatory activity was demonstrated in murine macrophages, primary human keratinocytes and an ex vivo human skin model through the attenuation of inflammatory responses. The formulation also showed cytocompatibility in murine macrophages, human keratinocytes and human dermal fibroblasts. Collectively, these findings provide early proof-of-concept for the feasibility of reformulating abrocitinib into a localized topical liposomes-in-hydrogel delivery system with prolonged drug release, skin retention and anti-inflammatory activity under the investigated experimental conditions. This supports further investigation of Ab-Lip-Hyd as a topical delivery approach for abrocitinib, although in vivo pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies, including direct assessment of JAK/STAT signaling, efficacy, repeated-dose safety and systemic exposure, are required to establish its therapeutic relevance.

articles.title: Targeted hypoxia-responsive small-molecule supramolecular carrier for tumor-selective doxorubicin delivery.
articles.abstract: Small-molecule supramolecular carriers provide structurally defined and highly tunable alternatives to conventional nanocarriers, but their limited passive tumor accumulation remains a major obstacle to effective drug delivery. Here, we developed an arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD)-modified, hypoxia-responsive sulfonated azocalix[4]arene (pep-SAC4A) as an actively targeted supramolecular carrier for doxorubicin (DOX). DOX was incorporated through reversible noncovalent host-guest complexation, preserving the original drug structure while enabling stimulus-triggered release. The azo-containing supramolecular host underwent structural cleavage under hypoxic/reductive conditions, resulting in disruption of the host cavity and release of DOX. RGD modification enhanced integrin-mediated cellular uptake and promoted intracellular trafficking from lysosomes to the nucleus. Under hypoxic conditions, pep-SAC4A/DOX induced greater mitochondrial dysfunction and DNA damage than the non-targeted formulation. In tumor-bearing mice, pep-SAC4A/DOX exhibited enhanced tumor accumulation and produced the strongest inhibition of tumor growth, accompanied by increased apoptosis, reduced proliferation, and lower interindividual variability in serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that active targeting and hypoxia-responsive release can be integrated into a small-molecule supramolecular host, providing a compact strategy for improving tumor-selective chemotherapy.

articles.title: Design of high dose lopinavir loading self-nanoemulsifying drug delivery systems using supersaturation and solidification strategies.
articles.abstract: Lopinavir (LPV) is a clinically relevant antiretroviral drug that is challenging to optimally formulate and deliver due to its low solubility and poor permeability. Self-nanoemulsifying drug delivery systems (SNEDDS) offer potential for LPV but suffer from low loading levels and instability. Here we employ supersaturation and solidification to improve these challenges. Optimised LPV-loaded liquid-SNEDDS (Capmul® PG8:Labrasol®:propylene glycol, 80:15:5 w/w) were supersaturated using a heating and cooling method at loading levels 80%, 150% and 200% of the LPV equilibrium solubility. Solid-SNEDDS were prepared by physical adsorption of liquid-SNEDDS onto different silica carriers (Parteck® SLC, Aerosil® R974, and Aerosil® 300). The biorelevant solubilisation properties were evaluated using two-stage dissolution and fed vs fasted lipolysis. Compared to crystalline LPV, liquid-SNEDDS increased LPV release 9-fold and 5-fold in gastric and intestinal dissolution, and 3-fold and 6-fold under fasted and fed lipolysis, respectively. Solidification altered the release and sustained LPV solubilisation, i.e. a progressive sustained release from Parteck® SLC, slow attenuated release from Aerosil® R974 and rapid release from Aerosil® 300. Together, these findings demonstrate that increased LPV loading can reduce formulation burden while retaining substantial biorelevant performance, but that performance following solidification is strongly dependent on silica carrier architecture.

articles.title: Preferential API loss during dry granulation milling for ribbons containing high concentration of polyethylene oxide.
articles.abstract: This study evaluated API loss during dry granulation of push-pull osmotic tablet active layer formulations. Two formulations, one containing polyethylene oxide, mannitol, and API, and another containing only polyethylene oxide and API, were roller compacted to form the active layer of the bilayer tablet. Unacceptable API loss and processability issues were observed between dry granulation and compression for mannitol-free formulations across multiple campaigns, roll forces, batch sizes and drug loads. Two hypotheses were investigated further: mannitol-API interactions that increase API retention in the mannitol-containing formulations, or the difficulty of impact-milling a highly concentrated, ductile-polymer-based formulation. In addition, remediations for assay loss are proposed for dry-granulating polyethylene oxide formulations.

articles.title: Formulation-controlled redaporfin cellular-targeted photodynamic therapy sensitizes tumors to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade via immunogenic cell death.
articles.abstract: Redaporfin is a clinically advanced photosensitizer developed for vascular-targeted photodynamic therapy (V-PDT), yet its therapeutic utility under long drug-to-light interval, cellular-targeted PDT (C-PDT), remains limited despite substantial tumor exposure. Here, we show that formulation-dependent control of redaporfin photochemistry and ER-associated intracellular localization can convert otherwise non-curative C-PDT into an effective partner for immune checkpoint blockade. Encapsulation in Pluronic®-based micelles prolonged the redaporfin triplet-state lifetime over sevenfold relative to ethanol and over twentyfold relative to a non-micellar aqueous environment, while preserving oxygen accessibility. Direct comparison with Pluronic® F127 demonstrated carrier-specific effects: despite greater cell-free ROS generation, F127 showed lower encapsulation efficiency, poorer storage stability, and inferior intracellular ROS generation and phototoxicity. P123 enhanced ER-associated redaporfin accumulation at 24 h and amplified an ICD phenotype, evidenced by increased calreticulin exposure and HMGB1 release; P123-mediated C-PDT also activated macrophages with an M1-like marker profile and induced adaptive PD-L1 upregulation in surviving CT26 cells. In vivo fluorescence imaging confirmed rapid tumor accumulation and sustained retention of redaporfin/P123 at 24 h. Whereas C-PDT alone and α-PD-L1 monotherapy were non-curative, combination with PD-1 and/or PD-L1 blockade produced durable complete responses in up to 50% of mice. All complete responders remained tumor-free during 120-day follow-up, and dual blockade conferred protection against CT26 rechallenge, providing functional evidence of long-term antitumor immune memory. These findings establish formulation-driven control of intracellular photochemistry and subcellular localization as an underappreciated determinant of PDT-mediated anticancer immunity and provide a translational strategy for repurposing a clinically advanced V-PDT photosensitizer for durable photodynamic immunotherapy.

articles.title: Lactiplantibacillus plantarum alleviates Parkinson's disease progression by reducing enteroendocrine α-synuclein aggregation in a rotenone-induced mouse model.
articles.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder driven by α-synuclein (α-syn) aggregation and accumulation. Recent evidence suggests that gut dysbiosis may trigger α-syn accumulation in the enteric nervous system, which spreads to the brain via the vagus nerve. Restoring the gut microbial balance through probiotic intervention offers a promising strategy to mitigate gut-origin pathology in PD. Lactiplantibacillus plantarum PS128 (PS128), a probiotic strain with neuroprotective properties, has shown neurotherapeutic benefits in PD models and patients; however, its mechanisms remain unclear. In a rotenone-induced PD mouse model, we found that PS128 supplementation significantly improved motor deficits and gastrointestinal dysfunction, reversed enteroendocrine cell (EEC) hyperplasia in the proximal colon (PC), and reduced α-syn accumulation in both intestinal and brain tissues. Notably, phosphorylated α-syn levels were significantly elevated in EECs, the myenteric plexus, and the substantia nigra, and these elevations were reversed by PS128. Furthermore, using real-time calcium imaging in a zebrafish model, we demonstrated that PS128 directly activates EECs. Transcriptomic profiling of the PC revealed calcium signaling and vitamin D metabolism as the major pathways modulated by PS128. Consistent with the transcriptomic findings, biochemical analyses demonstrated that PS128 increased serum calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. Moreover, 16S rRNA sequencing and correlation analysis revealed that PS128 modulated gut microbiota composition in PD-like mice, with changes in specific taxa correlating with α-syn burden and calcium regulation. Taken together, our findings suggest that PS128 alleviates PD-like pathology through modulation of the gut-brain axis and provide mechanistic insights into the neuroprotective actions of probiotics.

articles.title: Contribution of angiotensin receptor type II to dermal extravasation caused by bradykinin in mice: Implications for sartan-induced angioedema.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: While non-allergic angioedema induced by ACE inhibitors and sacubitril are caused by reduced bradykinin degradation and over-activation of bradykinin receptor type 2 (B2), the pathophysiology of sartan-induced angioedema is not fully understood. As angiotensin II receptor (AT) type 1 blockers (sartans) increase circulating angiotensin II, enhanced activation of AT2 by angiotensin II likely occurs. The aim of this study was to investigate whether the AT2 agonist compound 21 (C21) inhibits ACE activity and increases bradykinin-induced dermal extravasation. METHODS: Increased plasma angiotensin II by telmisartan was measured at a dose that reduced systolic blood pressure by 20 mmHg. C21 was synthesized and its biological activity assessed by vasorelaxation of aortic rings of control mice which was absent in rings of AT2-/y mice. As for Miles Assays AT2-/y mice were backcrossed to C57BL/6 J (AT2-/y-C57). Blood pressure remained unchanged by C21. RESULTS: In Miles assays in C57BL/6 J, but not in AT2-/y-C57, C21 potentiated dermal extravasation induced by bradykinin that was inhibited by the AT2 antagonist PD123319, while extravasation by the ACE resistant B2 agonist labradimil remained. Pre-treatment of human endothelial cells with C21 strongly reduced ACE activity in cell homogenates in an AT2 dependent manner suggesting a cellular loss of ACE and indicating reduced tissue ACE activity. Correspondingly, increased ACE activity in plasma occurred following treatment with C21. CONCLUSION: These data suggest an increase of bradykinin-induced skin extravasation due to direct AT2 activation which may contribute to explaining the molecular mechanism underlying the occurrence of sartan-induced non-allergic angioedema.

articles.title: Cyclical heat strain alters the function of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes in rats.
articles.abstract: Environmental conditions are frequently recognized as modifiers of xenobiotic toxicity, yet temperature as a driver of xenobiotic absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination is poorly understood. The present study investigated whether an environmentally relevant model of heat strain that accounts for day/night cycle shifts in temperature results in a pharmacokinetic phenoconversion by altering cytochrome P450 (P450)-mediated drug metabolism. Using a novel rat model designed to induce sustained, sublethal heat strain, we evaluated physiological adaptations, hepatic P450 expression and activity, and in vivo disposition of multiple isoform-specific probe substrates. Heat strain, measured by internal temperature, produced systemic physiological changes, including decreased body weight and increased water intake. Ex vivo assessment of hepatic microsomes revealed isoform-specific effects on P450 activity. Cyp1a2 and Cyp2e1 activity were reduced by heat strain, whereas Cyp2b6, Cyp2c22, and Cyp2d1 were unchanged and Cyp3a1 exhibited a nonsignificant downward trend. Consistent with reduced Cyp2e1 activity, in vivo pharmacokinetic analysis demonstrated increased systemic exposure and decreased elimination of the muscle relaxant, chlorzoxazone, along with delayed formation and prolonged retention of its primary Cyp2e1-specific metabolite, 6-hydroxychlorzoxazone. However, other P450-specific substrates demonstrated an apparently nonenzymatic shift in volume of distribution (Vd), indicating that heat strain impacts disposition through more than enzyme activity alone. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that heat strain produces isoform-specific alterations in P450 function and complex, systems-level changes in xenobiotic disposition. This work provides mechanistic support for the concept of climate-induced transient phenoconversion and highlights the need to further investigate heat strain as a modifier of drug metabolism and toxicity. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: As heat waves are becoming more common across the globe, it is imperative that we begin assessing how this shift in climate can impact human health. This work identifies heat strain as a driver of interindividual variability in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination, potentially putting people who live in high-heat environments at greater risk of drug and chemical toxicity due to altered P450-mediated metabolism.

articles.title: Multi-Objective Optimization of Population-Level Dosing Regimens.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Drug treatment optimization involves multiple competing objectives, including efficacy, toxicity, resistance, and cost. It is further complicated by interindividual variability that can make standardized regimens suboptimal for individual patients. We developed a population pharmacokinetics- pharmacodynamics (PKPD)-based framework to optimize dosing regimen at the population-level while accounting for interindividual variability, covariate distributions, and clinical expert input. METHODS: The framework optimizes treatment design parameters, including dose and dosing frequency, to maximize population attainment of treatment objectives. Individual attainment of these objectives is estimated using a population PKPD model and quantified into a penalty metric to enable multi-objective dose regimen optimization. Clinical expert input is incorporated through two approaches: 1) multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA)-based objective weight assignment and 2) gate optimization, an approach to search for a treatment design for which target attainment is equal to or greater than a reference treatment across all objectives. RESULTS: The framework was evaluated in case studies to highlight how this approach can support complex treatment design, incorporate clinical expert input, and integrate covariate information. Grid search evaluation confirmed that the framework identifies solutions close to the expected location of the global optimum. CONCLUSION: The presented framework is adaptable to diverse patient and disease contexts and supports population-level, model-informed dosing optimization.

articles.title: Beyond ratings: a condition-aware natural language processing framework for drug effectiveness decomposition, regulatory benchmarking, safety signal detection, and adversarial robustness assessment using patient-generated reviews.
articles.abstract: Patient-generated drug reviews offer a large source of real-world evidence on perceived medication effectiveness, yet existing computational analyses predominantly model effectiveness as a single drug-level estimate, ignoring variation across therapeutic indications. This study introduces an integrated four-module natural language processing (NLP) framework that extends patient review analytics from aggregate rating prediction toward condition-aware pharmacovigilance support. Module 1 decomposes drug effectiveness across 1880 drug-condition pairs (623 drugs; 131 conditions), showing that the same medication can differ by up to 4.18 rating points across indications (mean cross-condition range = 0.98 rating points on a 1-10 scale among the 533 drugs observed in at least two conditions). A condition-aware model combining term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features with linear support vector regression (SVR) achieves a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.749 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.731-0.767), comparable to a drug-level model (R2 = 0.744), while providing indication-specific estimates. Item-based collaborative filtering imputes unobserved drug-condition pairs with a hold-out root mean squared error (RMSE) of 0.716, no better than a simple additive drug + condition baseline. Module 2 benchmarks patient-derived scores against documented U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) safety actions for 230 matched drugs. FDA-actioned drugs were rated slightly higher (Cohen's d =  - 0.297, 95% CI - 0.431 to - 0.163; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) = 0.592), but this difference was largely explained by their much higher review volume: it disappeared with unshrunk ratings (d =  - 0.045) and was attenuated after covariate adjustment (odds ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.95-1.31), although a small difference persisted among drugs with at least 50 reviews (d =  - 0.285). Module 3 constructs a composite safety concern score from four lexicon-based dimensions. The score discriminated FDA-actioned drugs modestly (AUC = 0.568, 95% CI 0.516-0.619), including among drugs with at least 50 reviews (AUC = 0.593) and with corrected lexicon matching (AUC = 0.574); discontinuation language was the most consistent discriminating feature. The module flags 141 "blind-spot" drugs combining high ratings with high safety-concern language; many flags reflected lexicon terms that name the treated condition, so blind spots are hypothesis-generating only. Module 4 evaluates robustness to simple text perturbations and template-based fake review injection. TF-IDF with SVR and TF-IDF with Ridge regression yield robustness indices of 0.991 and 0.994, respectively; approximately 50 (SVR) and 61 (Ridge; extrapolated) injected reviews were required to shift a prediction by one rating point for sparsely reviewed target drugs. Condition-aware effectiveness estimates and linguistic safety signals can complement, but not replace, established pharmacovigilance sources.

articles.title: Intracellular glutathione availability, rather than vitamin C supplementation, determines endothelial cell resistance to water-soluble cigarette smoke toxicants.
articles.abstract: Smoking involves chronic exposure to cigarette smoke toxicants, which is associated with the development of vascular disease characterized by endothelial dysfunction. We examined the role of glutathione and vitamin C in antioxidant defense in endothelial cells exposed to water-soluble cigarette smoke toxicants. Exposure to cigarette smoke-conditioned medium decreased cell viability in a concentration and time-dependent manner, with rapid glutathione depletion and recovery. Cells exposed to non-lethal concentrations recovered their glutathione levels in a manner related with enhanced cell survival, and disruption of glutathione metabolism with L-buthionine-(S,R)-sulfoximine (BSO) drastically decreased cellular resistance to cigarette smoke toxicity and increased cell death. These negative effects were augmented in cells treated with graded hydrogen peroxide concentrations following exposure to cigarette smoke-conditioned medium. Intracellular vitamin C did not provide sustained protection against cigarette smoke toxicity and did not enhance glutathione recovery following oxidative challenge. Moreover, exposure to cigarette smoke-conditioned medium failed to affect the transport of reduced (ascorbic acid) or oxidized (dehydroascorbic acid) vitamin C by endothelial cells, regardless of the status of intracellular glutathione or vitamin C. We conclude that glutathione and vitamin C possess overlapping but clearly distinct functions in the response of cells to oxidative challenge. Specifically, in endothelial cells exposed to soluble cigarette smoke toxicants, glutathione was the major determinant against cigarette smoke toxicity.

articles.title: Metformin promotes apoptosis of senescent chondrocytes by disrupting the Bcl-xL/Mcl-1-Bak interaction.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The accumulation of senescent chondrocytes (SEC) beyond the body's tolerance capacity is a key contributor to osteoarthritis (OA) pathogenesis. Metformin (Met), a first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes, has shown therapeutic potential in various diseases. This study aims to explore the therapeutic effects and underlying mechanisms of Met in OA. METHODS: Cellular senescence was induced in immortalized human chondrocytes using doxorubicin (Dox), confirmed by β-galactosidase staining and western blotting. The effects of Met on SEC viability, mitochondrial membrane potential, and apoptosis were assessed. Protein expression and interactions were analyzed by western blot and live-cell fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) analysis. RESULTS: Met promoted death of SEC and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential, inducing caspase- and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-dependent apoptosis. Met upregulated Bak and Bim expression, downregulated Mcl-1, and activated Caspase-3, Caspase-8, and Caspase-9, leading to PARP cleavage. FRET analysis revealed that Met disrupted Mcl-1/Bak and Bcl-xL/Bak binding while facilitating Bim-Bak interaction, promoting Bak dimerization. DISCUSSION: This study provides the first evidence that Met induces apoptosis of SEC by reducing Mcl-1-Bak and Bcl-xL-Bak interactions while enhancing Bim-Bak binding, suggesting a novel therapeutic strategy for OA by targeting senescent chondrocytes through mitochondrial apoptosis pathways.

articles.title: Exogenous carnitine can modulate oxaliplatin sensitivity in colorectal cancer cells in vitro.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The clinical management of colorectal cancer (CRC) is hampered by the frequent development of oxaliplatin (OXA) resistance. This study investigated whether exogenous L-carnitine (CAR) modulates OXA sensitivity in CRC cells and whether any such effect depends on fatty acid oxidation (FAO). METHODS: The effects of carnitine, with or without OXA, on cell viability, proliferation, migration, oxygen consumption, apoptosis, cell-cycle distribution, and intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) were evaluated in HCT116 parental cells and an OXA-resistant subline (HCT116/L), using CCK-8, colony formation, wound healing, Seahorse XF analysis, flow cytometry, and ROS fluorescence probes. RESULTS: In vitro, exogenous carnitine dose-dependently reduced CRC cell viability, proliferation, migration, and respiration, and promoted apoptosis. Co-treatment with carnitine partially attenuated the anti-proliferative and pro-apoptotic effects of OXA in HCT116/L cells, consistent with reduced chemosensitivity. This effect was accompanied by a partial restoration of fatty-acid-dependent respiration and a reduction in OXA-induced ROS accumulation. CONCLUSION: In OXA-resistant HCT116/L (MSI-H) cells, exogenous carnitine is associated with reduced OXA sensitivity, an effect that requires fatty acid oxidation. These findings identify carnitine-FAO metabolism as a potential determinant of OXA response; whether limiting carnitine availability can restore OXA sensitivity in vivo remains a hypothesis to be tested.

articles.title: Pharmacist-led redesign of chemotherapy delivery and supportive care: effects on infusion capacity, aseptic workload, costs and resource stewardship in oncology practice.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Medication-related processes in oncology are complex and resource intensive, creating opportunities for treatment delays, preparation burden, medication errors, and inefficient resource utilization. Pharmacist-led interventions have been associated with improvements in medication safety, efficiency, and costs, yet evidence evaluating their system-wide impact remains limited. This study evaluated an integrated pharmacist-led, multidisciplinary redesign of medication-use processes encompassing supportive medications, infusion administration, and drug preparation in a tertiary oncology center. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We performed a retrospective analysis of routinely collected administration data from January to June 2023. Baseline practice (3,750 administrations) was compared with a modelled full-implementation scenario. Scheduled administration time (SAT) was used as an operational measure of infusion-unit resource use. Aseptic workload, direct acquisition costs, and assessed single-use consumable waste were estimated using prespecified model rules, measured unit weights, and 2023 institutional acquisition prices. A pragmatic February 2026 substudy compared current SAT with real administration time, reconstructed baseline equivalent SAT, and modelled full-implementation SAT. RESULTS: Baseline cumulative SAT was 8,945 h. IV supportive medications accounted for 1,801 SAT h and 680 h of aseptic preparation time. In the modelled full-implementation scenario, total SAT decreased by 43% (-3,851 h), aseptic workload by 666.8 h, direct acquisition costs by €20,276, and assessed single-use consumable waste by 331.6 kg. In the February 2026 substudy, current SAT closely approximated real administration time and indicated that a substantial proportion of the modelled SAT reduction had already been achieved in routine practice. DISCUSSION: To our knowledge, this is the first study to simultaneously quantify infusion service capacity, aseptic workload, direct costs, and consumable waste within a pharmacist-led, multidisciplinary oncology redesign framework. By streamlining medication-use processes across multiple stages of care, such interventions may contribute to safer medication delivery, improved resource stewardship, and greater infusion service capacity. This model represents a scalable and policy-relevant approach to supporting high-quality cancer care while promoting long-term healthcare sustainability.

articles.title: BL-DVDMS-mediated photodynamic therapy induces oxidative response associated with cellular senescence via p53/GADD45A signaling in lung cancer.
articles.abstract: Current chemotherapy options for lung cancer (LC) are limited by poor tumor selectivity, systemic toxicity, and acquired resistance. Photodynamic therapy (PDT) offers a promising minimally invasive modality as a potential conservative or complementary approach, yet its clinical adoption has been constrained by suboptimal photosensitizers and unclear mechanisms. This study investigated a novel PDT regimen combining a 450 nm blue laser with the photosensitizer sinoporphyrin sodium (DVDMS) to address these limitations in LC. Our findings demonstrate that BL-DVDMS treatment selectively inhibits lung cancer cell proliferation while sparing normal bronchial epithelial cells. Low-dose PDT induces a moderate oxidative stress response, leading to DNA damage and G2/M cell cycle arrest. Importantly, this treatment triggers a senescence-associated phenotype, evidenced by increased SA-β-Gal activity and elevated secretion of SASP factors (IL-6, IL-8), accompanied by altered p53/GADD45 A signaling. These effects are abrogated by ROS scavenging or p53 inhibition, indicating that the oxidative response plays a central role in the observed antitumor activity. In the subcutaneous xenograft model, this regimen significantly suppresses tumor growth with no detectable systemic toxicity. Collectively, this work identifies BL-DVDMS-mediated PDT as a mechanistically defined, senescence-associated therapeutic strategy. This study provides a potential complementary treatment option for inoperable LC patients, particularly for managing residual disease and enhancing existing therapies.

articles.title: Transferrin restrains rather than drives neuronal ferroptosis after intracerebral haemorrhage.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The transferrin-transferrin receptor axis is the principal route by which neurons acquire iron, and it is generally regarded as a driver of ferroptosis: transferrin receptor 1 is used as a ferroptosis marker, and blocking transferrin-bound iron uptake is protective in several models of iron-dependent injury. That framework predicts that transferrin should be harmful after intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH), a condition defined by catastrophic iron overload. Clinical observations point the other way, since patients with higher circulating transferrin have smaller haematomas and better outcomes. METHODS: We resolved this contradiction using bidirectional, neuron-targeted manipulation of transferrin in a rat autologous-blood model of ICH. Transferrin was silenced or overexpressed in neurons with adeno-associated virus given 3 weeks beforehand, the same manipulations were applied to hemin-exposed differentiated PC-12 neurons, transcriptomes were sequenced, and recombinant apo-transferrin was given intraperitoneally 1 h after ICH at 4, 10 or 20 mg/kg. RESULTS: Endogenous transferrin increased two- to threefold in perihaematomal neurons and microglia, peaking on day 3, the same time point at which ferroptotic injury was maximal. Silencing neuronal transferrin did not protect; it increased perihaematomal iron, hydrogen peroxide, and malondialdehyde; shrank neuronal mitochondria further; and enlarged the lesion. Overexpression produced the mirror image, driving iron below sham levels and halving neurodegeneration. Inversion was reproduced in hemin-exposed PC-12 neurons. Transcriptionally, transferrin did not reinforce antioxidant defence. It abolished the need for it. Hemin moved 6,976 genes in wild-type neurons but only 343 in transferrin-overexpressing ones, a 95% collapse of the injury programme. Across the 6,974 hemin-responsive genes, the effect of transferrin ran opposite to the effect of hemin (Pearson r = -0.869), reversing 99% of the genes that both perturbations moved significantly. The hemin-induced oxidative stress programme, including the HO-1/SLC7A11/TXNRD1 module, returned towards baseline. Recombinant apo-transferrin given 1 h after ICH reproduced these effects with a sharp threshold at 20 mg/kg, halved lesion volume, and restored sensorimotor and cognitive function at 14 days. DISCUSSION: We propose that ICH inverts transferrin's function: confronted with heme-derived iron that bypasses the transferrin cycle, transferrin is repurposed from an iron donor towards a high-affinity extracellular iron sink. Its buffering capacity, rather than iron load itself, sets the threshold for neuronal ferroptosis. That capacity is exhaustible, saturating well below what the injured brain requires.

articles.title: Label-free comparative proteomic analysis reveals distinct profiles of direct oral anticoagulants in human endothelial cells.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs) are the first-line treatment for thromboembolism prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation. Clinical and preclinical studies suggest that, beyond their anticoagulant properties, DOACs may have additional vascular effects. However, their effects on endothelial protein-abundance profiles remain incompletely characterized. The objective of this study was to explore the protein-abundance profiles associated with exposure of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) to each of the four DOACs in the absence of external stimuli, using a label-free quantification (LFQ) methodology. METHODS: Cultured HUVECs were exposed for 6 h to concentrations selected to approximate reported therapeutic plasma concentrations of apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran. All experiments were carried out in serum-free media, after a starvation period of 18 h. After protein extraction using the TRIzol Reagent, label-free quantitative proteomic analysis was performed using nanoLC-MS/MS, followed by the identification of differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) and bioinformatic enrichment analyses. RESULTS: We identified 1,643 protein entries, of which 753 were differentially abundant. Of these, 32 showed higher abundance and 26 showed lower abundance than the vehicle control in all four DOAC comparisons. Proteins showing shared abundance changes were mapped to gene identifiers that were enriched for annotations related to autophagy and cardiac development, and cellular activation. Several proteins showing abundance changes in all three FXa-inhibitor comparisons, but not in the dabigatran comparison, were mapped to annotations related to hypoxia response, vascular permeability, and cholesterol homeostasis. However, this comparison is potentially confounded by the absence of an HCl-matched vehicle control for dabigatran. The majority of DAPs were drug specific, with distinct signatures for each DOAC. Exploratory enrichment subnetworks linked mapped gene identifiers from drug specific protein sets to ontology terms including endothelial-cell chemotaxis, sodium-ion transport, necrotic cell death, mRNA splicing, and regulation of gene expression. These cellular functions were not directly measured. CONCLUSION: Under the experimental conditions used, exposure to the four DOACs was associated with common and drug-specific protein-abundance patterns in HUVECs. These protein-abundance patterns provide hypothesis-generating observations for subsequent functional investigation.

articles.title: High prevalence of adverse drug reactions among oral contraceptive pill users in Western India: a prospective observational study.
articles.abstract: Oral contraceptive (OC) pills are among the most widely prescribed hormonal preparations globally, yet prospective adverse drug reaction (ADR) surveillance data from the Indian subcontinent remain sparse. This prospective observational study aimed to estimate the prevalence, spectrum, and temporal pattern of ADRs among OC pill users at a tertiary care gynecology outpatient department and affiliated private clinics in Pune, Western India. A total of 201 women aged 18-60 years prescribed OC pills for contraceptive or non-contraceptive indications were enrolled; 130 were new initiators and 71 were existing users. Participants were followed for 3 months, with ADRs documented at three pre-specified time points anchored to the date of OC pill initiation. Of 201 participants, 179 (89.05%; 95% Wilson confidence interval: 83.98%-92.66%) experienced at least one ADR, with a mean of 1.87 ± 1.06 ADRs per participant. Nausea was the most frequently reported ADR (62.69%), followed by weight gain (25.87%), breast pain (24.88%), vomiting (22.39%), and headache (19.90%). A notable 87.06% of participants used OC pills for non-contraceptive therapeutic purposes, with polycystic ovary syndrome as the predominant indication (36.82%). Among new initiators, a distinct biphasic temporal pattern was observed: early-onset gastrointestinal ADRs-particularly nausea and vomiting-resolved completely by the third month, while weight gain emerged as a persistent late-onset effect. On multivariable analysis, reported weight gain was independently associated with baseline overweight/obese status rather than with polycystic ovary syndrome or OC pill formulation. Serious ADRs were rare, with no thromboembolic events recorded. These findings demonstrate a high ADR burden among OC pill users in an Indian clinical setting, predominantly driven by transient gastrointestinal symptoms, and highlight the importance of anticipatory counseling on the biphasic ADR trajectory, and prospective pharmacovigilance in guiding individualized prescribing.

articles.title: Jiegeng decoction ameliorates COPD-like pulmonary injury in association with changes in PPARγ expression, arachidonic acid metabolism, and gut microbial composition.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Jiegeng Decoction (JGD) is a classic traditional Chinese medicinal formulation that consists of Platycodon grandiflorus (Jacq.) A. DC. and Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch. This formulation was first recorded in the "Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases" during the Eastern Han Dynasty. Clinically, JGD has been employed as a fundamental prescription in the clinical management of various pulmonary disorders. Unlike previous studies, which focused primarily on the addition and subtraction prescriptions derived from JGD, the present study first sought to investigate the associated mechanisms and identify the principal bioactive metabolites of this foundational prescription for the treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)-like pulmonary injury, with particular attention to its underexplored effects on the intestine. METHODS: A cigarette smoke/lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced rat model of COPD-like pulmonary injury was used to assess the effects of JGD on pulmonary and intestinal injury. This assessment utilized histological staining, immunofluorescence, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. To explore and validate the underlying mechanisms and bioactive metabolites, lung transcriptomics, untargeted metabolomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, UPLC‒Q‒Orbitrap‒MS/MS, and LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages were utilized. RESULTS: An animal study revealed that JGD mitigated pulmonary histopathological damage, mucus hypersecretion, and the release of inflammatory cytokines in rats exposed to cigarette smoke/LPS-. Comprehensive transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses suggested that JGD may ameliorate inflammatory responses by modulating arachidonic acid metabolism, potentially through the upregulation of PPARγ expressions. Additionally, JGD alleviated intestinal injury and inflammation, restored the expressions of the barrier-associated proteins MUC2 and ZO-1, and was associated with alterations in the composition of the gut microbiota. Notably, specific microbial taxa were significantly correlated with pathological indicators and arachidonic acid metabolites. A total of 156 JGD-derived metabolites were detected and annotated in JGD, 77 of which were absorbed into the bloodstream. Among these compounds, liquiritigenin (LG) has emerged as a potential bioactive metabolite that can interact with PPARγ. In vitro studies demonstrated that both JGD and LG mitigated LPS-induced inflammation in RAW264.7 cells by restoring PPARγ expressions. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of PPARγ using GW9662 significantly reduced these protective effects, supporting the involvement of PPARγ signaling in LG-mediated inflammatory regulation. CONCLUSION: JGD may mitigate COPD-like pulmonary injury through a multitarget approach associated with the upregulation of PPARγ expressions, the modulation of arachidonic acid metabolism, the restoration of intestinal barrier-associated protein expression, and changes in the gut microbial composition. The LG within JGD may serve as a bioactive metabolite that contributes to these therapeutic effects.

articles.title: Association of trilaciclib use with hematologic outcomes during perioperative immunochemotherapy in resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: a prospective observational cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perioperative immunochemotherapy is a key treatment strategy for resectable esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression (CIM) may compromise treatment delivery. Trilaciclib, a transiently acting, reversible cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitor, has shown myeloprotective effects in advanced solid tumors; however, evidence in perioperative ESCC is limited. This study investigated the association between trilaciclib use and hematologic outcomes during perioperative immunochemotherapy.
